values.value: Notes on the Model Context Protocol, and why it is changing how AI tools get things done.

value.markup: Welcome! This little blog is built and filled entirely through MCP servers, which seems like the right way to celebrate them. Read on for two short posts on why the protocol is such a big deal.

documents.name: Why MCP Is Awesome
documents.path: WWW / MCP Blog / Why MCP Is Awesome

values.value: One open protocol, plugged into every tool: why the Model Context Protocol is the missing piece between AI assistants and the systems they need to work with.

value.markup:
Every few years a standard comes along that quietly makes a whole category of work disappear. The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is one of those standards. It gives AI assistants a single, open way to discover and use the tools around them, instead of a pile of bespoke integrations.

If you have ever wired an assistant up to a database, a ticket system and a CMS, you know the pain: three APIs, three authentication schemes, three sets of glue code. MCP replaces that with one contract that every tool and every assistant can speak.

values.value: One protocol, many connections. Photo by Conny Schneider on Unsplash.

value.markup:
First, MCP is open. Anyone can publish a server, and anyone can build a client. There is no single vendor to ask permission from, which is exactly why the ecosystem has grown so quickly: file systems, databases, browsers, design tools and content management systems all have servers today.

Second, MCP is self-describing. Each server lists its tools with names, descriptions and typed inputs, so an assistant can work out what is possible without a human writing a prompt for every action.

values.value: Build the integration once, and every assistant can use it.
The MCP idea in one sentence

value.markup: Finally, MCP lowers the cost of trying things. Spinning up a new connection takes minutes rather than a sprint, so experiments that were never worth the plumbing suddenly are. That is why so many people are enthusiastic about it, and why this post was published through it.

documents.name: MCP Makes Tools Talk
documents.path: WWW / MCP Blog / MCP Makes Tools Talk

values.value: MCP Makes Your Tools Talk to Your AI
Stop writing one-off integrations. With MCP your CMS, your database and your build tools all speak the same language to your AI assistant.

value.markup:
The real magic of MCP is not any single tool. It is that the tools finally share a vocabulary. A server announces what it can do, what inputs each action needs and what comes back, and the assistant simply reads that menu and gets on with the job.

That means the effort you spend exposing a system once pays off for every assistant that ever connects to it. No more rewriting the same adapter for each new AI product that shows up.

values.value: Everything connected to everything else. Photo by Alina Grubnyak on Unsplash.

value.markup:
Take a content management system as an example. Through an MCP server an assistant can list document types, create pages, add blocks and publish them, all using the same permissions a human editor would have. The CMS stays in charge of validation and security, and the assistant just asks nicely.

Because each server is small and focused, you can give an assistant exactly the tools a job needs and nothing more. A schema builder gets one set of tools, an editor gets another, and neither can wander into the other's territory.

values.value: Small servers, sharp tools, one shared language.
A good rule of thumb for MCP

value.markup: So if your tools still feel like islands, give MCP a try. Point an assistant at one server, watch it discover what is on offer, and then add the next. Before long the islands are a connected archipelago, and your AI is a genuine colleague rather than a chat window.
